newsitem.title: FRANCE: French reform said to paralyse military until 2000.
newsitem.headline: French reform said to paralyse military until 2000.

text.p: French military chiefs have told the government that a vast overhaul of the armed forces now under way will seriously curb their capacity for long-range action until the year 2000, the newspaper Le Monde wrote on Tuesday.

The well-informed daily said army chiefs reported that the reforms decided by President Jacques Chirac meant they would temporarily be unable to field more than 20,000 men at a time for overseas action and that participation in a Gulf War-type scenario was out of the question for up to four years.
The defence ministry was not immediate available for comment on the Le Monde report.
Chirac, who took power in May 1995, pushed through his modernisation plan precisely to increase the military's capacity for long-term actions overseas.

France has launched a series of military actions abroad in the past decades, including sending troops to ex-Yugoslavia, Cambodia, Somalia, Rwanda and Lebanon. But the existence of a mixed army of professionals and conscripts has posed major organisational problems.

The pivotal point of the reforms is to end conscription, which has existed for more than 200 years, and turn the military into all-professional forces since conscripts cannot be used outside Europe without parliamentary approval.
The forces, which now number over half a million, would be reduced to about 350,000 under the reforms, but all could be on instant call for combat duty abroad.
